question: When an X-ray photon interacts with matter, which interaction describes it being deflected in another direction with no loss of energy?
explanation: In pure scatter the photon is deflected in another direction without losing any energy.

question: What is the only difference between gamma rays and X-rays?
options: Gamma rays occur naturally, whilst X-rays are man-made
Gamma rays have high energy, whilst X-rays have low energy
X-rays travel in straight lines, whilst gamma rays do not
X-rays are ionising, whilst gamma rays are non-ionising
explanation: Gamma rays and X-rays are the same thing; the only difference is that gamma rays are naturally occurring and X-rays are man-made.
extraWrong: X-rays can travel in a vacuum, whilst gamma rays cannot
Gamma rays can damage tissue, whilst X-rays cannot
X-rays occur naturally, whilst gamma rays are man-made

question: Electromagnetic photons with medium energy are experienced as which of the following?
explanation: Very low energy photons make up radio waves, whilst medium-energy photons are visible to us as light.

question: Which of the following is NOT a property of X-rays?
options: They travel in straight lines from the source
They can travel through a vacuum
They can be detected by human senses
They can blacken film emulsion to create an image
explanation: X-rays cannot be detected by any human sense, which is one reason they must be treated with care.
extraWrong: They originate at the atomic level
They have a short wavelength and high energy

question: How does the severity of tissue reaction (deterministic) effects relate to the radiation dose?
options: It bears no relation to the dose
It depends only on the patient's age
It is proportional to the dose
It is the same at every dose
explanation: Tissue reaction effects result from high doses, and the severity of the damage is proportional to the radiation dose.
extraWrong: It decreases as the dose increases
It depends only on the area exposed
It is a matter of chance alone

question: Genetic stochastic effects of ionising radiation occur in which cells?
options: Normal body (somatic) cells of the face and jaw
Hard-tissue cells of the tooth enamel
Cells of the soft tissues lining the mouth
explanation: Genetic effects happen to the reproductive cells (egg and sperm), and damage may show up in future offspring.

question: What are the main aims of radiation protection?
options: Completely prevent stochastic effects and limit the severity of deterministic effects to an acceptable level
Completely prevent both deterministic and stochastic effects, whatever the size of the radiation dose
Completely prevent deterministic effects and limit the chance of stochastic effects to an acceptable level
Limit deterministic effects only, because the chance of stochastic effects cannot be reduced at all
explanation: Radiation protection aims to completely prevent deterministic effects and to limit the chances of stochastic effects to an acceptable level.
extraWrong: Completely prevent stochastic effects and ignore deterministic effects, which can never occur
Limit the severity of stochastic effects and the chance of deterministic effects to an acceptable level
Completely prevent stochastic effects by never exceeding a set safe dose of radiation

question: Which X-ray interaction with matter involves the photon passing straight through without touching anything?
explanation: In transmission the photon passes straight through the matter without touching anything.

question: When an X-ray photon hits matter and is deflected in another direction with a loss of energy, what is the interaction called?
explanation: Absorption and scatter is when the photon hits the matter and is deflected with a loss of energy; pure scatter involves no energy loss.

question: At what level do X-rays originate and interact with matter?
explanation: X-rays originate at the atomic level and also interact with matter at the atomic level.

question: For somatic stochastic effects, increasing the radiation dose increases the chance of damage occurring.
explanation: Stochastic effects are chance effects: the severity bears no relation to dose, but a higher dose increases the chance of damage.

question: Dental radiography uses radiation doses high enough to cause tissue reaction (deterministic) effects.
explanation: Dental radiography never uses radiation doses high enough to cause tissue reaction (deterministic) effects.

question: X-rays have a long wavelength and high energy.
explanation: X-rays have a short wavelength and high energy.

question: Although very unlikely, a single X-ray photon has the potential to cause a fatal cancer, so there is no such thing as a safe dose of radiation.
explanation: Stochastic effects can follow any dose, even a single photon, which is why there is no such thing as a safe dose.

question: Genetic effects are likely to result from dental radiography because the X-ray beam is often aimed at the reproductive organs.
explanation: Genetic effects are very unlikely in dental radiography because the X-ray beam is never aimed at the reproductive organs.

question: What is a single packet of X-ray energy called?
explanation: An X-ray is a packet of energy called a photon, and an X-ray beam contains millions of them.

question: Which interaction occurs when an X-ray photon hits matter and all of its energy is absorbed?
explanation: In absorption the photon hits the matter and all of its energy is absorbed; in absorption and scatter it is deflected with some loss of energy.

question: How does the severity of damage from somatic stochastic effects relate to the radiation dose?
options: It bears no relation to the radiation dose
It is proportional to the radiation dose
It is greatest at the lowest radiation doses
It depends only on the exposure time used
explanation: For stochastic (chance) effects the severity bears no relation to the dose, although a higher dose increases the chance of damage occurring.
extraWrong: It doubles whenever the radiation dose doubles
It depends only on the kV setting used
It is fixed by the type of film used

question: Which types of electromagnetic radiation have high energy and are classified as ionising radiation?
explanation: X-ray and gamma ray photons have high energy compared with other electromagnetic radiation and are classified as ionising radiation; radio waves and visible light are lower energy.

question: If an x-ray photon passes straight through the patient without touching them, we say it has been...
explanation: X-rays can pass straight through without touching anything. Never stand in the path of the x-ray beam.

question: What type of radiation are x-rays?
explanation: X-rays can be thought of as an extremely intense form of light. So strong it can pass through us but also cause damage.

question: How do you sense x-rays and detect them?
options: x-rays cannot be detected by human sense
explanation: X-rays are invisible.

question: Which effects of x-rays principally concern the dental profession?
explanation: B = X-ray beam never points at reproductive cells. A + D = doses from dental X-rays aren't strong enough. C = chances of causing damage to cells.
